## Learning Outcomes

Yesterday: one `.qmd` → a branded PDF. Today, the other axis: **one file to many**. You will be able to:

- **structure** several `.qmd` files into one Quarto **project** with shared configuration (`_quarto.yml`).
- **build** a navigable, **branded website** with within-page cross-references.
- make its builds **reproducible**, produce a **publishable folder**, and put it online.

By the end: the same penguins data, a set of pages (**including yesterday's report**) grown into a
**website your team can publish**.

::: notes
- **Say:** "Yesterday: one `.qmd` to a branded PDF. Today: many files, one project, then publish."
:::

## How today works

**Same shape as yesterday**: two rounds of **watch → follow along → your turn**, each ending in a
**Challenge** in the lab (solutions folded in), with a **break** between the rounds.

Watch for the **Follow along** / **Your turn** callouts: they flag every switch.

::: notes
- **Say:** "Same rhythm as yesterday: follow along, then your turn."
- **Don't announce a duration here.** Each "Your turn" callout carries its own "regroup in ~N min",
  which is where the room needs it.
:::

# Part 1: Build and structure a project {.center}

From one file to a whole site.

## Why a *project*? {#why-project}

::: {.callout-note title="Follow along"}
Open your editor: from here we build one project together.
:::

One `.qmd` renders alone. A **project** is a folder Quarto treats as one unit (shared config, one
build, one output folder):

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
``` {.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
# at the project root
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: _site # everything renders here
format:
  html:
    toc: true       # set once, every page gets it
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.incremental}
- `quarto render` builds the **whole** folder, not one file.
- Header options set **once** apply to every page.
- **`output-dir`**: the folder where the built site is written (`_site` by default). Publish *that*.
:::
:::
::::

::: aside
Quarto uses the **nearest `_quarto.yml`** up the tree as the project root: you add one to
`day2-projects/`, and nothing sits above it, so that folder *is* your project.
:::

::: notes
- **Say:** "Many files, one project. Open your editor."
- **Do:** add a minimal `_quarto.yml`; render the whole folder.
- **Say:** "This is how the pages of your team project connect."
:::

## Directory metadata: `_metadata.yml` {#metadata}

Yesterday a header set the defaults and a cell overrode them. `_metadata.yml` is that **same idea,
one scope wider**: options for every page in a **folder**, so you don't repeat them in each header:

``` {.yaml filename="analysis/_metadata.yml"}
# applies to every .qmd in analysis/
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
format:
  html:
    code-fold: true
```

Same narrow-wins rule, now across files: **document header** > `_metadata.yml` > `_quarto.yml`.
Set defaults wide, override narrow.

::: aside
Today's lab project is flat (a couple of pages at the root), so there's no folder to scope. Reach for
`_metadata.yml` when a **subfolder** of pages shares options.
:::

**Learn more:** [Directory metadata](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/quarto-projects.html#directory-metadata)

::: notes
- **Say:** "Same precedence rule as yesterday, now across project, folder, page, and cell."
- **Do not re-teach:** widen the rule only.
:::

## Websites: pages and navigation {#websites}

You already set `type: website`, which makes the folder a **site**: its pages share one navbar and
sidebar. You describe that navigation once, and Quarto builds it:

``` {.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
website:
  title: "Penguin Lab"
  # top bar — one entry per page
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: analysis.qmd
        text: Analysis
  # side menu, built from the files
  sidebar:
    contents: auto
```

. . .

`contents: auto` even builds the sidebar from the folder, so you don't hand-list pages.

::: {.aside}
**Listings** turn a folder of pages into an auto-generated index (a blog, a gallery of reports) via
`listing:` on a page. One slide's worth, more in the linked resources.
:::

**Learn more:** [Websites](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/) ·
[Listings](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-listings.html)

::: notes
- **Do:** add navbar and sidebar; render and show navigation.
- **Say:** "List navbar entries, or let `contents: auto` build a sidebar."
- **Next:** independent pages explain the cross-reference rule.
- **Watch for:** links are relative to source files, not `_site`.
:::

## Cross-references across a project {#xrefs}

::: {.callout-warning title="Eyes up — not a live *Follow along*"}
The next few slides are concept, no need to type along.
:::

Within **one page**, `@fig-`, `@tbl-`, `@eq-` resolve to a numbered, linked reference, exactly as
on Day 1. (Section headings work the same way with `@sec-`.)

. . .

Across **different website pages**, they do **not** auto-number: a website renders each page on its
own, so link between pages with ordinary Markdown links and the **navbar/sidebar** instead:

``` markdown
See the [analysis page](analysis.qmd) for the model.
```

::: {.callout-note title="Project-wide numbering is a *book*"}
If you need "Figure 3.2" to resolve *across* chapters, that's `type: book`: Quarto renders a book as
one unit with global numbering. A **website** keeps per-page numbering.
:::

**Learn more:** [Cross-references](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html) ·
[Book cross-references](https://quarto.org/docs/books/book-crossrefs.html)

::: notes
- **Before session:** confirm that a website does not resolve a cross-page `@fig-` reference.
- **If asked — does `@sec-` need `number-sections: true`?** No. The reference resolves either way
  (verified, Quarto 1.10). The option adds the number on the heading, which is why the docs pair
  them. This site sets it in `_quarto.yml`, so a demo here shows numbers a participant's own bare
  document will not.
:::

## One brand → the whole project: `_brand.yml` {#brand}

Yesterday, `_brand.yml` branded one **Typst PDF**. Drop that **same file at the project
root** and Quarto **auto-discovers** it (no header line, no per-page config):

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
``` {.yaml filename="_brand.yml"}
color:
  palette:
    teal: "#4C979F"
  primary: teal
typography:
  fonts:
    - family: Albert Sans
      source: google
  base:
    family: Albert Sans
```
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
- **Every page and every deck** inherits it from that one root file, so you never name it in a page.
- Add a page later? Branded on render, nothing to wire up.
- Need an exception? `brand: false` opts a page out. `brand: other.yml` points it elsewhere.

![](../images/brand-yml-wide-color.svg){width="300px" fig-alt=""}
:::
::::

**Learn more:** [Quarto brand](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/brand.html) ·
[brand.yml spec](https://posit-dev.github.io/brand-yml/)

::: notes
- **Focus:** one root `_brand.yml` scales yesterday's PDF branding to the project.
- **Do:** show the site before/after adding `_brand.yml`.
- **Say:** "Brand once at the project root, not once per page."
- **Do not reveal:** theme-layer order; it is the lab exercise.
- **Before session:** demo uses `[cosmo, brand]` or no named theme.
- **If asked:** plots need `theme_brand_ggplot2()`; `brand: false` opts out.
:::

## Your turn {#your-turn-1}

::: {.callout-tip title="Your turn — ~45 min, then a break"}
Head to the **[Lab](../../labs/quarto-projects/index.qmd#website-challenge)** and the **Website
Challenge**: turn a set of `.qmd` into a navigable, **branded website**: `_quarto.yml`, a navbar, and
the shared brand. ~45 min, then a **break**, back after.
:::

You can now structure files into a branded, navigable **website**. After the break we make its builds
reproducible and **ship** it.

::: notes
- **Say:** "Website Challenge: project, navigation, brand, folder options, then an optional listing.
  You have 45 minutes; we meet at 15:30."
- **Ask:** "Where did the HTML move?"
- **Ask:** "The font changed but the navbar did not. Why?"
- **Ask:** "You edited no `.qmd`; where did the option come from?"
- **Watch for:** wrong working folder; rendering one file; links aimed at `_site`.
- **Catch-up:** `solutions/day2/`.
:::

# Part 2: Scale and publish {.center}

Make builds reproducible, then publish: how your team ships its project.

::: notes
- **Say:** "You built the site. Now make its builds reproducible, then publish it."
:::

## Freeze: skip unchanged computations {#freeze}

::: {.callout-note title="Follow along"}
Back in your project's `_quarto.yml`.
:::

**freeze** was one line in Day 1. Compute can be slow: you don't want every prose edit to re-run a
20-minute model fit. Two tools, easily confused:

::: {.incremental}
- **`cache`**: the **compute engine's** cache, not Quarto's. It defers to *knitr* (R) or *Jupyter Cache*.
  Per-**cell**, kept until that cell's code changes, and it works in a **single document**.
- **`freeze`**: **Quarto's** switch for when a document re-executes.
  **Project-only**: rendering one file always runs it. Results live in `_freeze/`, refreshed only
  when its source changes. Commit it and **CI** *(the automated build)* rebuilds with **no R at all**.
:::

. . .

``` yaml
# _quarto.yml
execute:
  freeze: auto        # re-execute a document only when its source changes
```

**`freeze: auto`** is the setting to adopt. **`freeze: true`** hands you full control instead.

::: notes
- **Say:** "A prose edit should not rerun a 20-minute model."
- **Contrast:** cache = engine, per cell; freeze = Quarto, per document, project only.
- **Do:** add `freeze: auto`; change one page and render.
- **Payoff:** commit `_freeze/`; CI can build without R.
- **Next:** `freeze: true` gives manual control.
:::

## The `freeze: true` workflow {#freeze-workflow}

With **`freeze: true`**, a project build **reuses `_freeze/` even when the source changed**. You
refresh a page when you choose to, by rendering that one file (a single-file render always executes):

``` {.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
execute:
  freeze: true
```

``` bash
quarto render analysis.qmd     # runs the code, rewrites _freeze/ — commit it with your change
```

. . .

The loop: **edit a page → render that one file → commit `_freeze/`**. Once every page has been
frozen once, the project build and **CI** stay **R-free**. That's exactly how **quarto.org** itself
is built.

. . .

`freeze: auto` instead lets the *build* recompute a page whose source changed. Convenient, but
`true` keeps the trigger in your hands.

::: notes
- **Say:** "With `true`, only a direct document render recomputes the page."
- **Precision — don't say "never runs R".** A page with no `_freeze/` entry still executes, and so
  does a brand-new page added to the project (checked on Quarto 1.10). What `true` buys is that an
  **edited** page is not recomputed by the build. "R-free" is the steady state, once every page has
  been frozen once.
- **Do:** edit `analysis.qmd`; render that file; show `_freeze/` change. Then render the project.
- **Contrast:** `auto` recomputes changed pages; `true` requires manual refresh.
- **Example:** quarto.org uses `true` and commits `_freeze/`.
:::

## Reproducibility has two parts {#renv}

`freeze` pins the **results**. It doesn't pin **what produced them** (the package versions):

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **`freeze`** → `_freeze/`: do not repeat slow computation.
- **`renv.lock`** → *"pin the packages, so the team rebuilds the same environment."*
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
``` r
renv::init()       # once, to start tracking
renv::snapshot()   # write renv.lock
renv::restore()    # rebuild the same env
```
:::
::::

Together: a colleague (or CI) rebuilds the *same* site, with or without re-running the analysis.

**Learn more:** [renv](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/)

::: notes
- **Say:** "freeze pins results; `renv.lock` pins package versions."
- **Timing:** drop this first if short.
:::

## Publishing {#publishing}

The hands-on part is small: **render, then point a host at `output-dir`.**

``` bash
quarto render              # builds the whole project into _site/
```

- `_site/` is the whole deliverable. Point any static host at it (an internal server, your
  department's pages, a hosting service).
- **Posit Connect Cloud** takes it in one command, with a free account and **no repository**:

``` bash
quarto publish posit-connect-cloud
```

The first run opens a browser to sign in, then uploads the folder you just built.

::: {.callout-tip title="Your turn — optional, if we have time"}
Publish your site and open it on your phone. The lab has the steps. Everyone still leaves with
`_site/`, which is the deliverable either way.
:::

::: notes
- **Do:** run `quarto publish posit-connect-cloud` and show browser sign-in.
- **Say:** "`_site/` is the deliverable. This command puts it on a URL."
- **Mention:** free Posit account required; skipping loses nothing.
- **If asked:** scheduled and repository builds are also available.
:::

## Your turn {#your-turn-2}

::: {.callout-tip title="Your turn — regroup in ~45 min"}
Back to the **[Lab](../../labs/quarto-projects/index.qmd#ship-it-challenge)**, the **Reproducible Build
Challenge**: make the build skip unchanged pages, bring **yesterday's report** onto the site, and turn
it into a publishable `_site/` folder. The dashboard demo and publishing are optional.
:::

::: notes
- **Say:** "Reproducible Build Challenge: freeze the build and add yesterday's report. You have 45 minutes."
- **Ask:** "How can you prove the code did not run?"
- **Ask:** "Where do cache and freeze write results? Which folder do you commit?"
- **Celebrate:** the Day-1 report becoming a site page.
- **Catch-up:** `solutions/day2/`; fast finishers inspect the dashboard or publish.
:::

## What you can do now {#wrap-up}

You can now:

- structure `.qmd` files into a **project** with `_quarto.yml`, `output-dir`, and `_metadata.yml`.
- build a **branded website** with navigation and explain why cross-page references differ from a book.
- make builds **reproducible** (`freeze` + `renv.lock`), produce a **publishable `_site/`** for a host
  or CI, and put it online.

. . .

**You've built the two axes:** one document to a branded PDF (Day 1), one folder to a published site
(Day 2), with yesterday's report now a page of it. Everything your **team project** needs.

::: notes
- **Close with:** "Yesterday's document is now a page of today's site."
:::

## Demos (if time) {#demos}

Extra topics:

::: {.incremental}
- **Book versus website**: mostly the same machinery. Pick a **book** when you need one linear read with
  global numbering, a **website** otherwise. *(1 decision, not a new toolset.)*
- **Interactivity**: an **htmlwidget** (`plotly`, `leaflet`) is pure R and self-contained.
  **[OJS](https://quarto.org/docs/interactive/ojs/)** *(Observable JS, a browser-side, non-R path)*
  and **[Shinylive](https://quarto-ext.github.io/shinylive/)** *(Shiny running in the browser,
  no server)* are links, not live builds.
:::

::: notes
- **Timing:** cut from the bottom if fewer than 5 minutes remain.
- **If dashboards were skipped:** show the rendered dashboard for 30 seconds; name valueboxes,
  boxplot card, and tabbed panel.
:::

## Thank you! {.center}

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
